prompt: A dashboard using empirical nearest rank reports p99 latency of 420 milliseconds. Allowing ties, what does this mean?

options.explanation: A percentage threshold is not a count of 99 observations.

options.text: At least 99% of recorded observations are at or below 420 milliseconds.
options.explanation: The rounded-up rank and ties may put more than 99% there.

options.text: The slowest 1% have an average latency of 420 milliseconds.
options.explanation: That is a tail average, not a percentile threshold.

options.text: There is 99% confidence that the true mean is 420 milliseconds.
options.explanation: Percentiles describe spread; confidence concerns estimator uncertainty.

workedExample: Read the threshold in the sorted observations under the stated convention. It limits how many are above it but does not say how slow those remaining observations are or how precisely a population percentile is estimated.

prompt: A page waits for all required backend calls. Each has the same independent chance of being slow, strictly between zero and one. What happens when more such calls are added?

options.text: The chance of at least one slow call increases.
options.explanation: There are more opportunities to hit the tail while all calls remain required.

options.text: Only the average backend latency matters.
options.explanation: Waiting for all calls makes the slowest required result important.

options.text: The chance stays equal to a single backend’s tail chance.
options.explanation: That ignores the union of slow-call events.

options.text: Adding their probabilities always gives the exact page risk.
options.explanation: Overlapping slow-call outcomes are double-counted by the sum.

workedExample: A page avoids this delay only when every required call is fast. More independent calls reduce that all-fast probability. Take its complement for at least one slow call, and reconsider the model if backend delays are correlated.

prompt: A nearest-rank percentile implementation sorts a nonempty sample and selects an observation after rounding the percentage rank upwards. Why might it differ from another library on a small sample?

options.text: Sorting changes the actual measured latencies.
Nearest rank must return the mean.
options.explanation: It selects an observed value rather than averaging the sample.

options.text: A difference proves the population distribution changed.
options.explanation: Two methods can disagree on identical data.

options.text: The other library may interpolate using a different percentile convention.
options.explanation: There are multiple sample-quantile definitions, especially noticeable with few observations.

workedExample: Compare definitions before diagnosing a bug. Check rank calculation, zero-based indexing and whether the method interpolates. State the convention alongside a result, and remember that tiny samples give uncertain population-tail estimates.

prompt: Which methods can compute or explicitly approximate fleet p99 across servers over the same time window? Select all that apply.

options.text: Merge compatible quantile sketches and report their approximation limits.
options.explanation: Suitable sketches retain distribution information needed for approximate merging.
Those values omit traffic weights and the rest of each distribution.

options.text: Combine all raw observations and apply a specified percentile convention.
options.explanation: The complete sample supports an exact sample quantile.

options.text: Sum histograms with compatible bucket boundaries and estimate the percentile.
options.explanation: Merged counts preserve the combined distribution at bucket precision.

workedExample: A fleet percentile depends on the combined observation ranks, not a mean of thresholds. Preserve enough distribution information to combine counts or samples, while acknowledging representation and sampling uncertainty.
